newsitem.title: USA: AMD says Intel suit entirely on marketing.
newsitem.headline: AMD says Intel suit entirely on marketing.

text.p: Advanced Micro Devices Inc said that a trademark infringement suit filed against it by semiconductor giant Intel Corp is entirely about marketing and it does not prevent AMD from shipping its new processor that is compatible with Intel's MMX multimedia technology.

"There is no dispute about intellectual property rights," said a spokesman for Sunnyvale, Calif.-based AMD. "Even if we were to lose, which we hope we won't, they can't delay us from shipping to our customers. They can only require us to mention MMX according to their terms and conditions."
AMD shares dropped 2-3/4 after Intel said it filed a suit.

Traders said investors were afraid of another lengthy legal battle between Intel and AMD. The two were tied up in messy lawsuits for years over whether or not AMD had the intellecutal property rights to clone Intel's X86 processor architecture. AMD now has the right to develop clones of several Intel processors.
AMD said that Intel is likely using this trademark lawsuit to create fear, uncertainty and doubt among AMD's customers.
"There is a certain intimidation factor that they have attempted to use from time to time," said the AMD spokesman.

"Our fear is that their sales force will create fear, uncertainty and doubt among customers by saying if your customers buy this, we may have to rip those chips out of the socket," the AMD spokesman said.

He said that current marketing plans for AMD's K6 processor just describe it as an AMD K6 processor in its packaging. "We describe it as an MMX processor, but the chip just says its an AMD K6 processor."
AMD also said it uses its own implementation of MMX technology. MMX refers to Intel's multimedia extension technology that is introduced in January in the P55C chip.

AMD expects to begin shipping the K6 in the second quarter. AMD executives at the CeBIT show in Hanover, Germany said the K6 will begin appearing in PCs this summer and that several yet-to-be-named German PC makers would agree to use the K6 early next month.
AMD plans to price the chip below Intel's processors.

Thomas McCoy, general counsel for AMD, said later in a statement that Intel's claim of trademark rights to MMX, a term that is the generic acronym for "multimedia extensions," is the issue in the litigation.
"We believe the term MMX belongs to the public domain and we expect to prevail when the matter goes to trial," he said.
AMD said on April 2 that it will unveil its sixth- generation Microsoft Windows-compatible microprocessor to compete with Intel's Pentium Pro and forthcoming Pentium II chips.
"This case is really about advertising and marketing, which no doubt explains the timing of Intel's lawsuit," AMD said.
